claim: Acinetobacter baumannii has been identified by the WHO as a critical priority pathogen for new antibiotic development.
source: Acinetobacter baumannii is a Gram-negative bacteria that has been identified by the WHO as a critical priority pathogen for new antibiotic development.
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction without experimental data from this manuscript, representing established knowledge.

claim: A. baumannii was highlighted for its increasing role in nosocomial infections and its intrinsic resistance to multiple antibiotics.
source: A. baumannii was highlighted for its increasing role in nosocomial infections and its intrinsic resistance to multiple antibiotics.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about A. baumannii.

claim: Several virulence factors have been identified in Acinetobacter species including iron-uptake pathways.
source: Several virulence factors have been identified in Acinetobacter species including iron-uptake pathways (Peleg et al., 2012; Harding et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Iron is essential for all bacteria.
source: Iron is essential for all bacteria, and consequently, human pathogens have to possess an efficient acquisition system to scavenge iron from the host during infection.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bacterial physiology.

claim: Gram-negative bacteria secrete small molecules (siderophores), which chelate iron with extremely high affinity.
source: Gram-negative bacteria secrete small molecules (siderophores), which chelate iron with extremely high affinity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial iron acquisition.

claim: The resulting siderophore-iron complex is recognized by a specific outer-membrane transporter that couples to the TonB system to translocate the complex into the periplasm.
source: The resulting siderophore-iron complex is recognized by a specific outer-membrane transporter that couples to the TonB system to translocate the complex (and thus iron) into the periplasm where an ABC transporter takes it across the inner membrane (Noinaj et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The conserved and essential nature of the uptake system has drawn interest as a potential drug target.
source: The conserved and essential nature of the uptake system has drawn interest as a potential drug target.
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for research in the field.

claim: Several siderophore-conjugates have been developed to deliver drugs directly to the periplasm with promising results.
source: Several siderophore-conjugates have been developed to deliver drugs directly to the periplasm with promising results (Wencewicz and Miller, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Three classes of siderophore have been identified as being produced by A. baumannii: acinetobactin, fimsbactins and baumannoferrins.
source: Three classes of siderophore have been identified as being produced by A. baumannii, acinetobactin (Yamamoto et al., 1994), fimsbactins (Proschak et al., 2013) and baumannoferrins (Penwell et al., 2015) and each would be expected to be transported by distinct TonB-dependent transporters.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature identifying these siderophores.

claim: Analogues of the bis-catechol siderophore fimsbactin A linked to antibiotics such as loracarbef/ciprofloxacin have proven effective in killing A. baumanni.
source: Analogues of the bis-catechol siderophore fimsbactin A linked to antibiotics such as loracarbef/ciprofloxacin (Wencewicz and Miller, 2013), daptomycin (Ghosh et al., 2018) and cephalosporin (Liu et al., 2018) have proven effective in killing A. baumanni.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A. baumanni has been targeted by directly inhibiting the biosynthesis of acinetobactin.
source: A. baumanni has been also targeted by directly inhibiting the biosynthesis of acinetobactin (Drake et al., 2010; Neres et al., 2013) and by disrupting the acinetobactin uptake mechanism through the use of an oxidized version of acinetobactin (Bohac et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The acinetobactin system has been identified as a virulence factor in mouse infection models.
source: The acinetobactin system is of particular interest since it has been identified as a virulence factor in mouse infection models (Gaddy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Acinetobactin is synthesized as a precursor, preacinetobactin, which rearranges non-enzymatically and irreversibly at pH >7 to give acinetobactin.
source: Acinetobactin is synthesized as a precursor, preacinetobactin, which rearranges non-enzymatically and irreversibly at pH >7 to give acinetobactin (Figure 1A) (Sattely and Walsh, 2008; Wuest et al., 2009; Shapiro and Wencewicz, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: There have been different reports on whether acinetobactin or preacinetobactin or both are transported into the bacteria.
source: There have been different reports on whether acinetobactin or preacinetobactin or both are transported into the bacteria (Song et al., 2017; Shapiro and Wencewicz, 2017) complicating rational design.
evidence: This is supported by citations to conflicting previous literature.

claim: The A. baumannii outer-membrane transporter protein, BauA, has been identified as a vaccine candidate.
source: The A. baumannii outer-membrane transporter protein, BauA, that recognises this siderophore has itself been identified as a vaccine candidate (Esmaeilkhani et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The apo structure of BauA was solved to a resolution of 1.8 Å by single wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) using selenomethionine-labeled proteins.
source: The apo structure of BauA was solved to a resolution of 1.8 Å by single wavelength anomalous diffraction (SAD) using selenomethionine-labeled proteins.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used to determine the structure.

claim: Residues 33 to 703 of the protein are well defined in the electron density map.
source: Residues 33 to 703 of the protein are well defined in the electron density map, while the N-terminal region comprising the TonB box is missing, presumably because it is flexible.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystallographic data.

claim: BauA has the typical outer-membrane TonB-dependent transporter (TBDT) fold with a β-barrel formed by 22 antiparallel strands, several extracellular loops, and a plug domain folded inside of the barrel.
source: BauA has the typical outer-membrane TonB-dependent transporter (TBDT) fold with a β-barrel formed by 22 antiparallel strands, several extracellular loops, and a plug domain folded inside of the barrel (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The extracellular loops of the β-barrel form a large open cavity bordered by mainly short and apolar amino acids giving large access to the loops NL1-NL3 of the plug domain.
source: Compared to the other TBDTs, the extracellular loops of the β-barrel form a large open cavity bordered by mainly short and apolar amino acids giving large access to the loops NL1-NL3 of the plug domain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The closest structural homologues are ferrichrome and enantiopyochelin transporters.
source: Search of the structural database reveals the closest structural homologues are ferrichrome (Locher et al., 1998) (1by5, rmsd of 2.5 Å for 634 residues aligned and 2fcp, 2.4 Å for 631 residues) and enantiopyochelin (Brillet et al., 2011) (3qlb, rmsd of 2.5 Å for 630 residues) transporters.
evidence: This is based on structural database search and comparison with known structures.

claim: The asymmetric unit contains three monomers arranged around a threefold symmetry axis.
source: The asymmetric unit contains three monomers arranged around a threefold symmetry axis reminiscent of the porin arrangement (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) and thus plausibly biologically meaningful.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: PISA suggests a trimer with a high degree of confidence.
source: PISA (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007), a computational assessment of oligomeric state in the crystal, suggests a trimer with a high degree of confidence.
evidence: This is based on computational analysis using PISA software.

claim: Biophysical methods (gel filtration and light scattering) do not support a trimeric assembly.
source: Biophysical methods (gel filtration and light scattering) do not support a trimeric assembly.
evidence: This is based on experimental biophysical measurements.

claim: Size Exclusion Chromatography coupled to Multi-Angle Light Scattering (SEC-MALS) analysis in C8E4 is consistent with monomer.
source: Size Exclusion Chromatography coupled to Multi-Angle Light Scattering (SEC-MALS) analysis in C8E4 is consistent with monomer whilst native gel shows the protein runs more closely to a dimer; however, the detergent bound to the protein may increase the apparent weight suggesting a monomer in solution (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on SEC-MALS experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: When native protein crystals were incubated with preacinetobactin and acinetobactin compounds (both preloaded with Fe3+), the same structure was obtained in both cases: BauA bound to a heterocomplex Fe3+-preacinetobactin-acinetobactin (1:1:1).
source: We incubated separate native protein crystals with preacinetobactin and acinetobactin compounds (both compounds preloaded with Fe3+); surprisingly in both cases, we obtained the same structure: BauA bound to a heterocomplex Fe3+-preacinetobactin-acinetobactin (1:1:1) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on crystallographic soaking experiments and structure determination shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LC-MS analysis of preacinetobactin in the crystallization conditions shows that in the absence of iron, the majority of preacinetobactin is converted to acinetobactin in 30 min and no preacinetobactin was observed the next day.
source: LC-MS analysis of preacinetobactin in the crystallization conditions shows that in the absence of iron, the majority of preacinetobactin is converted to acinetobactin in 30 min and no preacinetobactin was observed the next day (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C); indicating that the presence of iron stabilizes preacinobactin.
evidence: This is based on LC-MS experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was a small amount (~2%) of preacinetobactin in the acinetobactin sample.
source: On the other hand, we discovered that there was a small amount (~2%) of preacinetobactin in our acinetobactin sample (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: After full conversion of preacinetobactin into acinetobactin, no crystal structure complex with BauA was obtained with this material.
source: After full conversion of preacinetobactin into acinetobactin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), no crystal structure complex with BauA was obtained with this material.
evidence: This is based on crystallization experiments with fully converted acinetobactin.

claim: The coordination of the iron is octahedral with four coordination atoms from preacinetobactin and two hydroxyls from acinetobactin.
source: The coordination of the iron is octahedral with four coordination atoms from preacinetobactin (one hydroxy group of the catecholate, the hydroxy of the hydroxamate, the nitrogen of the methyl oxazoline and one nitrogen (N1) of the imidazole group) and two hydroxyls from acinetobactin (the catecholate) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structure shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The protein interacts mainly with the preacinetobactin molecule.
source: The protein interacts mainly with the preacinetobactin molecule.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of protein-ligand interactions.

claim: BauA recognises the preacinetobactin through two direct hydrogen bonds between the hydroxamate group and Tyr312 of β7 and Arg253 of L3 and one interaction through a bridging water molecule between Asp375 and the nitrogen N2 of the imidazole.
source: BauA recognises the preacinetobactin through two direct hydrogen bonds between the hydroxamate group and Tyr312 of β7 and Arg253 of L3 and one interaction through a bridging water molecule between Asp375 and the nitrogen N2 of the imidazole, respectively (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of hydrogen bonding shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The binding site is predominantly hydrophobic in character with van der Waals interactions involving residues Trp97, Tyr125, Tyr314, Tyr378, Gly334, Gln335, Leu336, Arg379 and Leu684.
source: The binding site is predominantly hydrophobic in character with van der Waals interactions involving residues Trp97, Tyr125, Tyr314, Tyr378, Gly334, Gln335, Leu336, Arg379 and Leu684.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the binding site.

claim: The acinetobactin molecule makes only one hydrogen bond (Arg253) and one van der Waals interaction (Leu684).
source: The acinetobactin molecule makes only one hydrogen bond (Arg253) and one van der Waals interaction (Leu684).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of protein-ligand interactions.

claim: The experimental electron density is most convincingly fitted by a mixture of two diastereomers of acinetobactin.
source: The experimental electron density is most convincingly fitted by a mixture of two diastereomers of acinetobactin (Figure 2C), in an earlier co-crystalliszation experiment the 'wrong' diastereomer of acinetobactin was clearer (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F; Figure 2—figure supplement 2G.
evidence: This is based on analysis of electron density maps shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Fe3+-preacinetobactin binds to BauA with nM affinity whilst Fe3+-acinetobactin shows no binding.
source: These results are unambiguous: the Fe3+-preacinetobactin binds to BauA with nM affinity whilst Fe3+-acinetobactin shows no binding.
evidence: This is based on ITC experimental data.

claim: A stoichiometry of 1:1 Fe3+: preacinetobactin has a Kd of 763 nM.
source: A stoichiometry of 1:1 Fe3+: preacinetobactin has a Kd of 763 nM, whereas 1:2 Fe3+:preacinetobactin bind with 83 nM affinity.
evidence: This is based on ITC experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: 1:2 Fe3+:preacinetobactin bind with 83 nM affinity.
source: A stoichiometry of 1:1 Fe3+: preacinetobactin has a Kd of 763 nM, whereas 1:2 Fe3+:preacinetobactin bind with 83 nM affinity.
evidence: This is based on ITC experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In both cases, the stoichiometry of binding was one Fe3+ to one protein.
source: In both cases, the stoichiometry of binding was one Fe3+ to one protein; in neither case did we see any evidence for a biphasic recognition model that has been proposed between enterobactin and FepA (Payne et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on ITC experimental data.

claim: The titration reveals complexation of the free siderophore in the presence of low amounts of metal to give a complex of two siderophores to one metal, with the free siderophore almost disappearing when the metal reaches 0.5 molar equivalent.
source: The titration reveals complexation of the free siderophore in the presence of low amounts of metal to give a complex of two siderophores to one metal, with the free siderophore almost disappearing when the metal reaches 0.5 molar equivalent (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on NMR titration data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Two different new sets of resonances were observed, both with chemical shift distinct from the free siderophore, indicating two different ion coordination modes for each molecule of preacinetobactin in the ML2 complex.
source: Two different new sets of resonances were observed, both with chemical shift distinct from the free siderophore. This magnetic inequivalence clearly indicates two different ion coordination modes for each molecule of preacinetobactin in the ML2 complex.
evidence: This is based on NMR spectroscopy data.

claim: The formation constants were calculated as Kf(ML)=1.2·10^5 M−1; Kf(ML2)=7.2·10^3 M−1.
source: The formation constants were calculated as Kf(ML)=1.2·105 M−1; Kf(ML2)=7.2·103 M−1.
evidence: This is based on fitting NMR titration data to a complexation model.

claim: NMR shows that metal binding to acinetobactin results in the largest shifts of signals within the catechol group, whereas in preacinetobactin the largest shifts are observed in the central portion of the molecule, where the hydroxamate moiety is located.
source: NMR shows that metal binding to acinetobactin results in the largest shifts of signals within the catechol group, whereas in preacinetobactin the largest shifts are observed in the central portion of the molecule, where the hydroxamate moiety is located in agreement with the crystal structure (Figure 3C and Table 1).
evidence: This is based on NMR chemical shift analysis shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: BauA preferentially recognises preacinetobactin not acinetobactin.
source: We establish that BauA recognises preacinetobactin not acinetobactin.
evidence: This is based on structural, ITC, and NMR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Under the most likely physiological conditions, low iron and neutral pH, the mixed species (Fe3+-preacinetobactin-acinetobactin) would seem the most plausible compound for uptake.
source: Under the most likely physiological conditions, low iron and neutral pH, the mixed species would seem the most plausible compound for uptake.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biophysical data combined with knowledge of physiological conditions.

claim: In the crystal structure, preacinetobactin fits into a complementary pocket.
source: Structural biology strongly implies that BauA in fact recognizes preacinetobactin and not acinetobactin. In the crystal structure, preacinetobactin fits into a complementary pocket; a simple molecular model shows that the same site would not bind acinetobactin due to extensive van der Waals clashes with Tyr312 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and molecular modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The same site would not bind acinetobactin due to extensive van der Waals clashes with Tyr312.
source: In the crystal structure, preacinetobactin fits into a complementary pocket; a simple molecular model shows that the same site would not bind acinetobactin due to extensive van der Waals clashes with Tyr312 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on molecular modeling shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In the absence of Fe3+, preacinetobactin rapidly converts to acinetobactin under the crystallization conditions.
source: We observed that in the absence of Fe3+, preacinetobactin rapidly converts to acinetobactin under the crystallization conditions.
evidence: This is based on LC-MS analysis of preacinetobactin under crystallization conditions.

claim: The Fe3+ complex stabilized preacinetobactin by preventing the conversion to acinetobactin.
source: In our hands, the Fe3+ complex stabilized preacinetobactin by preventing the conversion to acinetobactin. This was also observed by NMR in solution with Ga3+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) and it agrees with the literature (Shapiro and Wencewicz, 2016).
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and supported by citation.

claim: The acinetobactin molecule is not itself recognised by the protein, rather it is the favorable coordination of the catechol group to the remaining two sites of Fe3+ that drives complex formation.
source: The acinetobactin molecule is not itself recognised by the protein, rather it is the favorable coordination of the catechol group to the remaining two sites of Fe3+ that drives complex formation.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis showing minimal protein-acinetobactin interactions.

claim: Based on the 1H-NMR experiment performed with Ga3+, at siderophore/iron ratio >0.8, the dominant complex is Fe3+-preacinetobactin (Fe3+L) whilst at siderophore/iron ratio <0.6, the Fe3+L2 is dominant.
source: Based on the 1H-NMR experiment performed with Ga3+, we predict that at siderophore/iron ratio >0.8, the dominant complex is Fe3+-preacinetobactin (Fe3+L) whilst at siderophore/iron ratio <0.6, the Fe3+L2 is dominant.
evidence: This is based on NMR titration data and modeling.

claim: ITC suggests that the Fe3+L2 binds to BauA with higher affinity than the Fe3+L complex.
source: ITC suggests that the Fe3+L2 binds to BauA with higher affinity than the Fe3+L complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on ITC data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under physiological conditions such as blood where free iron is very low, it is the heterotrimeric Fe3+-preacinetobactin-acinetobactin complex that is most likely to be bound by BauA and taken up.
source: Combining all our data, we suggest that under physiological conditions such as blood where free iron is very low, it is the heterotrimeric Fe3+-preacinetobactin-acinetobactin complex that is most likely to be bound by BauA and taken up (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is inferred from combining structural, ITC, and NMR data with knowledge of physiological conditions.

claim: Only under acidic conditions (pH <6), where preacinetobactin conversion is slower, is it conceivable that the Fe3+- (preacinetobactin)2 complex could be taken up.
source: Only under acidic conditions (pH <6), where preacinetobactin conversion is slower, is it conceivable that the Fe3+- (preacinetobactin)2 complex could be taken up.
evidence: This is inferred from the pH-dependent conversion of preacinetobactin to acinetobactin.

claim: A. baumannii infections do occur in an acidic environment.
source: This maybe significant as A. baumannii infections do occur in an acidic environment (Peleg et al., 2008; Higgins et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The structure suggests the uncoordinated nitrogen atom of the imidazole ring has the potential for modification without affecting recognition.
source: The crystal structure suggests the uncoordinated nitrogen atom of the imidazole ring has the potential for modification without affecting recognition.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis of the binding site.

claim: One of the oxygens and a carbon of catechol seem plausible candidates for expansion.
source: Similarly, one of the oxygens and a carbon of catechol seem plausible candidates for expansion (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The 2-OH of preacinetobactin is essential but changes at the 3 and 5 positions of the catechol are well tolerated.
source: Shapiro and Wencewicz (2017) and Song et al. (2017) reported important indications about the role of the different portions of both ligands by comparing the biological activity of multiple derivatives and checking complex formation through UV-vis spectroscopy. These studies confirm the 2-OH of preacinetobactin is essential but changes at the 3 and 5 positions of the catechol are well tolerated (no information on the four position was reported).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The structure suggests that there is no protein imposed recognition requirement on the second molecule.
source: The structure suggests that there is no protein imposed recognition requirement on the second molecule, this potentially unlocks a diversity of conjugate molecules complementing the fimsbactin A type conjugates (Wencewicz and Miller, 2013; Ghosh et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis showing minimal protein-acinetobactin interactions.

claim: Acinetobactin and preacinetobactin were synthesized following the synthetic schemes and the protocols described by Takeuchi et al., 2010.
source: Acinetobactin and preacinetobactin were synthesized following the synthetic schemes and the protocols described by Takeuchi et al., 2010.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for synthesis.

claim: The coding sequence of the mature protein BauA was amplified from the genomic DNA ATCC 19606.
source: The coding sequence of the mature protein BauA (uniprot Q76HJ9) was amplified from the genomic DNA ATCC 19606 using the primers 5'- AGGGGCGCCATGGCTGTTATTGATAATTCAACAAAAACTC and 5'- AATTTGGATCCTTAAAAGTCATATGATACAGATAGCATATACG and Pfu DNA polymerase.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for cloning.

claim: The proteins were over-expressed in E. coli C43 (DE3) cells.
source: The proteins were over-expressed in E. coli C43 (DE3) cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for protein expression.

claim: Crystals of BauA appeared at 20°C after a few days by mixing 1 μl of protein solution (10 mg.ml−1) with 1 μl of reservoir solution containing 10% PEG 8000, 0.1 M Hepes pH 7.5, 0.1M KCl, and 10% ethylene glycol.
source: Crystals of BauA appeared at 20°C after a few days by mixing 1 μl of protein solution (10 mg.ml−1) with 1 μl of reservoir solution containing 10% PEG 8000, 0.1 M Hepes pH 7.5, 0.1M KCl, and 10% ethylene glycol.
evidence: This describes the experimental crystallization conditions.

claim: Data were collected at the beamlines i02, i03 and i24 at the Diamond light source Oxfordshire.
source: Data were collected at the beamlines i02, i03 and i24 at the Diamond light source Oxfordshire.
evidence: This describes where the X-ray diffraction data were collected.

claim: Structure of BauA was solved by SAD with the program AUTO-RICKSHAW.
source: Structure of BauA was solved by SAD with the program AUTO-RICKSHAW (Panjikar et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the computational method used for structure solution.

claim: Atomic coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (6H7F, 6H7V, 6HCP).
source: Atomic coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank (6H7F, 6H7V, 6HCP).
evidence: This provides the PDB accession codes for the deposited structures.

claim: Affinity of BauA for Fe3+-preacinetobactin and Fe3+-acinetobactin were measured by isothermal titration calorimetry using a VP-ITC or a ITC200 instrument at 25 ˚C.
source: Affinity of BauA for Fe3+-preacinetobactin and Fe3+-acinetobactin were measured by isothermal titration calorimetry using a VP-ITC or a ITC200 instrument (GE Healthcare) at 25 ˚C.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for ITC measurements.

claim: 1H spectra were acquired at 300K with an Agilent UNITY INOVA spectrometer operating at a Larmor frequency of 500 MHz.
source: 1H spectra were acquired at 300K with an Agilent UNITY INOVA spectrometer operating at a Larmor frequency of 500 MHz.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used for NMR spectroscopy.

claim: Titrations were performed in acetate buffered saline (ABS) at pH five prepared in D2O (pD 5.4), at constant ligand concentration in the 2–3 mM range by varying metal concentration (Ga3+).
source: Titrations were performed in acetate buffered saline (ABS) at pH five prepared in D2O (pD 5.4), at constant ligand concentration in the 2–3 mM range by varying metal concentration (Ga3+), which was added in the form of Ga(ClO4)3.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for NMR titrations.
